about: CK-A, the Analyst checkpoint (ck-a-spreadsheet). Prairie Town High School is fictional; its load and several inputs are illustrative and labelled so in the log; the costs, prices, capacity factor and price index are dated public numbers (sources). The page's model recomputes every worked number, and the course's tests check it against this file and against the worked workbook's formulas.

case.fictional: Prairie Town and its high school are fictional; the school's load and several inputs are illustrative.
case.situation: Prairie Town High School's district is offered a rooftop solar array and a battery behind the school's meter.
case.deliverable: An auditable spreadsheet that tells the district what it would gain or lose, who else pays or benefits, and how sure that answer is.
facts: System
250 [[kw-dc|kW-DC]] of rooftop solar and a 150 kW / 300 kWh battery, installed together
School
uses 1,000,000 kWh a year, with a billed peak of 400 kW every month (illustrative)
Tariff

a [[demand-charge|demand charge]] of $10 per kW-month plus an energy charge, set so the school's bill averages Kansas's 2025 commercial price, 11.17 cents/kWh (EIA); exports earn 3 cents/kWh (illustrative)
Battery power
cuts the monthly billed peak by 60% of its power on average (illustrative)
Battery energy
about 200 [[full-cycle|full cycles]] a year, each taking in 300 kWh from the school's supply and returning 90%; the 10% lost is bought at the energy charge (illustrative)
Costs
from EIA's 2024 distributed-generation report (2022 dollars) and NLR's 2025 ATB (2023 dollars); convert to 2025 dollars
Money
25 years, real 2025 dollars, a 4% [[real-rate|real discount rate]] (the course's), battery replaced at the end of year 15
End value
at year 25 the replacement battery has 5 of its 15 years left: count 5/15 of its cost as its [[residual-value|residual value]] (straight line)
The utility
avoids 3 cents for each kWh it no longer supplies and, for half of the battery's peak cut, $180 per kW a year of capacity (illustrative; lesson A4's unit cost)
Rate reset
assume the utility recovers its whole remaining revenue shortfall from its other customers at the next rate reset

tasks.title: Your boundary
tasks.prompt: In two or three sentences: whose money does your main result count, over what period and in which dollars, and what does it leave out?
points: Whose money: the school district's, from its electricity bill, the system's capital, upkeep and the battery's replacement.
Time and money: 25 years, real 2025 dollars, one real discount rate (4%), with costs from other dollar years converted.
Left out, and said so: tax credits, financing, resilience, CO2's value and solar wear (or a stated subset of these).
The other parties (the utility's other customers, federal taxpayers, the resource view) reported apart from the main result.
tasks.solution: The school district's own money over 25 years in real 2025 dollars at 4%: its bill saving against the capital, upkeep and battery replacement. Left out: tax credits, financing, resilience, CO2's value and solar wear. Other customers and the resource view are reported apart.

tasks.title: Solar output
tasks.prompt: How much electricity does the array make in a year?

unitNote.kW: kW measures power; a year's output is energy: kWh or MWh per year.
unitNote.MW: MW measures power; a year's output is energy: kWh or MWh per year.

tasks.solution: 250 kW × 0.178 × 8,760 h = 389,820 kWh, about 390 MWh a year.

tasks.title: Up-front cost in 2025 dollars
tasks.prompt: What does the system cost up front, in 2025 dollars?

tasks.title: The school's bill saving
tasks.prompt: How much lower is the school's electricity bill in a year (gross: before upkeep)?
tasks.solution: Energy charges $18,624, export credits $2,924, demand charges $10,800, battery losses −$382: $31,965 a year.

tasks.title: The main result
tasks.prompt: Over 25 years at 4%, counting the brief's residual value, by how much does the present value of the school's costs exceed the present value of its savings? (If your model says the savings are larger, recheck it.)

answer.show: about $776,000: a net present value of −$776,000

tasks.solution: −$866,046 up front, + $265,465 of net savings ($16,993 a year × 15.62), − $226,820 for the replacement, + $51,077 of residual value: NPV −$776,324.

tasks.title: Who pays the gap
tasks.prompt: Part of the school's bill saving is not a saving in the utility's costs. Under the brief's rate-reset assumption, who pays it?
options: The utility's other customers, at the next rate reset
Nobody: every dollar the school saves is a real cost saved

why.a: The school receives this part: it is in its bill saving.
why.b: The utility still has to recover its costs; under the brief's assumption, the next rate reset moves the gap onto other customers' rates.
why.c: No tax credit is counted here; a credit would be a separate transfer.
why.d: The utility avoids only its energy and capacity costs, less than the bill saving.

tasks.solution: Under the brief's assumption, the utility's other customers, at the next rate reset: a [[transfer|transfer]], not a real cost saved. Until a reset, or if the utility does not recover it all, part stays with the utility.

tasks.title: The cost shift
tasks.prompt: Under the same assumption, how much a year moves to the utility's other customers?
tasks.solution: Bill saving $31,965 − the utility's avoided cost $19,615 ($11,515 of energy, $8,100 of capacity) = $12,351 a year.

tasks.title: What moves the result most
tasks.prompt: Swinging one input at a time over the ranges in the worked log, which moves the school's NPV most?
options: The demand charge, $5 to $20 per kW-month, with the energy charge re-set so the pre-project bill is unchanged

why.a: The capital is the largest single number in the result.
why.b: The rate changes the weight of every future year and the replacement.
why.c: A higher demand charge raises the battery's saving; the energy charge falls to keep the pre-project bill, so the solar saves less. The two partly cancel.
why.d: Price moves the energy saving, a modest share of the total.

tasks.solution: The worked sensitivity sorts the swings: up-front cost first.

tasks.title: Your log and your sensitivity
tasks.prompt: Paste three rows of your assumptions log and your sensitivity statement (the main result as a range, and the input that moves it most).
points: Every input has a value, a unit, a type (sourced, course data, illustrative, choice, derived) and a source or a reason.
Sourced values name the document, the table or page, and an as-of date.
Costs from different dollar years are converted to 2025 dollars with a stated index.
The main result is given as a range from the sensitivity, with the input that moves it most named.
tasks.solution: Each input carries its value, unit, type, source and date; costs are in 2025 dollars by a stated index; the sensitivity reports the range and the largest swing.
